lines.text: An Amazon link can pay a creator up to 10% of your order.
lines.say: An Amazon link can pay a creator up to ten percent.

lines.text: The link carries the creator's tag, so the store knows who sent you.
lines.say: The link carries the creator's tag, so the store knows who sent you.

lines.text: On Amazon, a click counts for 24 hours, or up to 89 days for items added to your cart in that window.
lines.say: On Amazon, a click counts for twenty-four hours, or eighty-nine days for items carted in that window.

lines.text: Amazon's standard rates (Oct 2026) run from 0% on gift cards to 10% on luxury beauty; many categories pay 1-4.5%.
lines.say: Amazon's standard rates run from zero on gift cards to ten percent on luxury beauty. Many categories pay one to four and a half percent.

lines.text: Example: a $200 order in a 4% category pays the creator $8 ($200 x 4%).
lines.say: So a two hundred dollar order in a four percent category pays the creator eight dollars.

lines.text: Your price? Usually the same. The store pays that $8 as a marketing cost.
lines.say: Your price? Usually the same. The store pays that eight dollars as a marketing cost.

lines.text: The FTC's Endorsement Guides, updated in 2023, say creators should clearly disclose paid links.

lines.text: Amazon makes creators post this line, so when you see it, their Amazon links can earn them a cut.

post.title: How an Amazon link can pay a creator up to 10% of your order
post.ig:
An Amazon link can pay a creator up to 10% of your order.
Amazon counts a click for 24 hours (items added to cart in that window: up to 89 days).
Amazon standard rates (Oct 2026) run from 0% (gift cards) to 10% (luxury beauty); many categories pay 1-4.5%.
Example: $200 order in a 4% category = $8 to the creator. Your price is usually the same.
The FTC's Endorsement Guides (updated 2023) say creators should clearly disclose paid links.
Sources: Amazon Associates Central, FTC Endorsement Guides (16 CFR Part 255).
